name: O'Connell Monument
address: O'Connell Street Lower, Dublin 1
historical_description: Bronze monument to Daniel O'Connell, conceived by John Henry Foley in 1866 and completed by Thomas Brock in 1883. It includes a high-relief frieze and multiple figures around a granite plinth.
historical_significance: Major national monument at the southern entrance to O'Connell Street.
access_status: Public realm; check temporary event restrictions.
photography_brief: Full monument from front and sides

name: General Post Office (GPO)
address: O'Connell Street Lower, Dublin 1
historical_description: Neoclassical post office designed by Francis Johnston, with a six-column Ionic portico. Built 1814–1818, damaged during the 1916 Easter Rising and reconstructed in the 1920s. NIAH describes surviving physical traces including bullet marks.
historical_significance: Headquarters of the 1916 Easter Rising and major civic landmark.
access_status: Public exterior; interior access subject to operating hours and venue rules.
photography_brief: Full façade from across O'Connell Street
Six Ionic columns and portico ceiling

name: GPO historic cast-iron lantern bases and wheel guards
address: In front of the General Post Office, O'Connell Street Lower, Dublin 1
historical_description: Pair of cast-iron lantern-post bases and six domed wheel-guards recorded by NIAH. Lantern bases are described as likely early nineteenth-century; wheel-guard date is less certain.
historical_significance: Rare surviving early nineteenth-century street furniture associated with the GPO.
access_status: Public realm; avoid obstructing pedestrians.

name: Famine Memorial — Rowan Gillespie
address: Custom House Quay, Dublin 1
historical_description: Six bronze figures by Rowan Gillespie, erected in 1997. The figures carry bundles and face east along Custom House Quay. Bronze commemorative plaques are set among granite paving stones around the group.
historical_significance: Public memorial commemorating the Great Famine and the suffering and emigration associated with it.
access_status: Public quayside; check temporary works and riverfront conditions.
photography_brief: Bundles, clothing, faces and dog figure

name: Bronze name plaques within the Famine Memorial paving
address: Granite-sett surround of Famine Memorial, Custom House Quay, Dublin 1
historical_description: NIAH describes bronze commemorative plaques dispersed among granite setts around the sculpture. Individual plaques and inscriptions require on-site transcription and photographic verification.
historical_significance: Names form part of the memorial composition; individual wording must be transcribed from legible photographs.
access_status: Public quayside; do not step onto restricted surfaces.
photography_brief: Record plaque position relative to figures

name: The Custom House
address: Custom House Quay, Beresford Place, Dublin 1
historical_description: Neoclassical custom house designed by James Gandon. Construction began in 1781. Gutted by fire in May 1921 during the War of Independence and restored in 1926–1929. NIAH attributes exterior carvings to Edward Smyth.
historical_significance: One of Dublin's major neoclassical civic buildings and a key War of Independence site.
access_status: Public exterior; interior access subject to OPW opening and photography rules.

name: Henry Grattan Monument
address: College Green, Dublin 2
historical_description: Bronze statue by John Henry Foley, erected in 1876 on a dressed limestone pedestal. NIAH also records two former gas-lamp standards with carved seahorses to the east.
historical_significance: Commemorates the politician associated with the campaign for legislative independence.
access_status: Traffic island; photograph only from safe pedestrian viewpoints.

name: Thomas Davis Monument and Fountain
address: College Green, Dublin 2
historical_description: Bronze statue by Edward Delaney, erected in 1966. Includes circular fountain with four bronze figures, panels depicting famine and scenes from Davis's poetry, and an inset footpath plaque.
historical_significance: Commemorates Irish writer and nationalist thinker Thomas Davis (1814–1845); occupies the site of the former William of Orange statue.
access_status: Traffic island; use safe public pedestrian viewpoints only.

name: George Salmon Statue
address: Trinity College Dublin, north of the Campanile, College Green, Dublin 2
historical_description: Seated white Galway-marble statue erected in 1911 and moved to its present position in 1964. NIAH describes a limestone plinth with incised lettering.
historical_significance: Commemorates George Salmon (1819–1904), Provost of Trinity College from 1888 to 1904.
access_status: Trinity College campus; check visitor access and photography policy.

name: Lecky Statue
address: Trinity College Dublin, Library Square, Dublin 2
historical_description: Cast-bronze seated figure of W. E. H. Lecky, cast by Sir William Goscombe John and erected in 1906 on a carved granite plinth.
historical_significance: Commemorates Irish historian and political theorist W. E. H. Lecky (1838–1903).
access_status: Trinity College campus; check visitor access and photography policy.

name: Edmund Burke Statue
address: Trinity College Dublin, north of main entrance, College Green, Dublin 2
historical_description: Standing electro-typed copper-bronze figure by J. H. Foley, erected in 1868 on a stepped granite plinth with incised lettering.
historical_significance: Commemorates Edmund Burke (1729–1797), Dublin-born political thinker and Trinity alumnus.
access_status: Trinity College campus; check visitor access and photography policy.

name: Cactus Provisoire — Alexander Calder
address: Fellows Square, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin 2
historical_description: Welded and riveted painted sheet-steel sculpture by Alexander Calder, cast in 1967 and installed at Trinity in 1978. It stands in a cobbled circular setting with an inscribed limestone plaque.
historical_significance: Nationally rated public artwork recorded by NIAH.
access_status: Trinity College campus; check visitor access and photography policy.

name: Reclining Figures — Henry Moore
address: Library Square, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin 2
historical_description: Freestanding abstract bronze sculpture by Henry Moore, erected in 1967 on a polished black-granite plinth in the north-west corner of Library Square.
historical_significance: Nationally rated modern sculpture contrasting with classical architecture.
access_status: Trinity College campus; check visitor access and photography policy.

name: City Hall (former Royal Exchange)
address: Cork Hill, Dublin 2
historical_description: Former Royal Exchange, built largely of Portland stone between 1769 and 1779 and now used as Dublin City Hall. NIAH rates the building of national significance.
historical_significance: Major eighteenth-century civic building associated with Dublin's commercial and municipal history.
access_status: Public exterior; interior subject to City Hall visitor rules.

name: Old Detective Office, 1 Exchange Court
address: 1 Exchange Court, Dublin 2
historical_description: Four-storey building formerly used as a Royal Irish Constabulary barracks and detective office associated with Dublin Castle. NIAH notes a commemorative granite plaque above the entrance and links to executions during the War of Independence.
historical_significance: Building with documented associations with policing and the revolutionary period.
access_status: Public street view; not a visitor attraction. Do not enter private premises.

name: Jim Larkin Monument
address: O'Connell Street Lower, outside the former Clerys building, Dublin 1
historical_description: Freestanding bronze figure of James ('Big Jim') Larkin with outstretched arms, designed by Oisín Kelly and erected in 1980 on a square-plan tooled granite pedestal. NIAH records gilt lettering and inset bronze plaques on the south, east and west faces.
historical_significance: Commemorates labour leader Jim Larkin and recalls his address to an illegal assembly from a hotel balcony during the 1913 Lockout.
access_status: Public street setting; photograph from the footpath without obstructing pedestrians or entering the carriageway.

name: Jim Larkin Monument pedestal inscription plaques
address: Three faces of the granite pedestal of the Jim Larkin Monument, O'Connell Street Lower, Dublin 1
historical_description: NIAH records inset bronze plaques on the south, east and west faces of the monument pedestal. The inscriptions include words attributed to Jim Larkin and commemorative commendations by Patrick Kavanagh and Seán O'Casey. Exact text and punctuation are to be transcribed from founder photographs.
historical_significance: The inscriptions form an integral documentary component of the monument and preserve quotations and literary tributes associated with the labour leader.
access_status: Public street setting; photograph from the footpath without obstructing pedestrians.

name: Talbot Street cast-iron P&T post box
address: Talbot Street, Dublin 1 (NIAH 50010137; verify exact pavement position in the field)
historical_description: Freestanding round-plan cast-iron post box with plinth base, raised P&T insignia, moulded neck, dentillated frieze and shallow domed cap. NIAH records a Carron Company, Stirlingshire maker's mark on the rear of the base.
historical_significance: Regional-rated example of early Irish state postal street furniture; the P&T insignia dates it to the early years of the Irish Republic.
access_status: Public footpath; do not obstruct postal operations or pedestrian movement.

name: Victorian cast-iron pillar post box, Gardiner Street Upper
address: Gardiner Street Upper, Dublin 1 (NIAH 50010760; verify exact pavement position in the field)
historical_description: Freestanding cylindrical cast-iron pillar box with flat-domed top and fluted collar. The shaft bears Queen Victoria's VR royal insignia; the base carries the maker's inscription A. HANDYSIDE & CO. LTD. DERBY & LONDON.
historical_significance: Regional-rated Victorian street object that remains in postal use and documents the design and manufacture of nineteenth-century cast-iron postal infrastructure.
access_status: Public footpath; avoid obstructing postal operations or pedestrians.
photography_brief: Full pillar box from front and side

name: 10 Talbot Street
address: 10 Talbot Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: NIAH records a terraced two-bay, three-storey former house with a later ground-floor shopfront. Surviving upper-floor features include Flemish-bond red brickwork, gauged brick segmental-headed window openings, granite sills, timber sash windows (some replacements) and a decorative brick eaves course.
historical_significance: One of the few Talbot Street buildings identified by NIAH as predating the destruction associated with the 1916 Rising; it retains Victorian fabric and contributes to the historic street terrace.
access_status: Photograph the public-facing exterior from the footpath; do not enter private premises without permission.
photography_brief: Full façade, including roofline and shopfront
research_notes: NIAH record and registration number identified; direct page retrieval was restricted during this research pass, so source details are retained as indexed NIAH record data and should be checked against the live register before publication.

name: Loop Line railway viaduct over Talbot Street
address: Talbot Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: Triple-span iron railway viaduct carrying the Loop Line over Talbot Street. NIAH describes a riveted steel girder span supported by fluted cast-iron cylindrical piers, with a bow-string panelled central parapet, star motifs and maker's insignia for A. Handyside & Co. Ltd.
historical_significance: A major surviving piece of late nineteenth-century railway engineering that links Connolly Station on the north side of the Liffey with the south-side rail network; its construction transformed the city skyline and remains part of the active transport system.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

research_notes: NIAH registration 50010134; grid reference retained as supplied. Active railway infrastructure: no access to tracks, bridge structure or restricted railway property.

name: Marlborough Street Edwardian post box
address: West side of Marlborough Street, Dublin 1, north of the Pro-Cathedral
historical_description: Freestanding cast-iron post box with shallow domed cap, moulded corona and neck, cylindrical shaft and moulded plinth. The hinged door carries a crown and RE VII POST OFFICE insignia; the plinth bears the maker's lettering McDowall Steven & Co London & Glasgow. NIAH notes that it is set within original granite kerbing.
historical_significance: A well-preserved Edwardian post box still in use, documenting late British-era postal infrastructure and historic granite street edging.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

name: 23 Marlborough Street
address: 23 Marlborough Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: Terraced two-bay, four-storey late eighteenth-century house with later ground-floor shopfront. NIAH records a double-pile slate roof, red-brick Flemish-bond walls, gauged brick window openings, granite sills and surviving sash-window features.
historical_significance: One of a small number of eighteenth-century buildings surviving on Marlborough Street; the upper façade retains an important historic composition despite alterations at ground level.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.
photography_brief: Window openings, sash boxes and granite sills
research_notes: NIAH registration 50010218; grid reference retained. Photograph only from public pavement; present commercial use may alter the ground-floor appearance.

name: 77 Marlborough Street
address: 77 Marlborough Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: End-of-terrace two-bay, three-storey red-brick house dating to c.1750, now in retail use. NIAH describes Flemish-bond brickwork, a pitched slate roof behind a parapet, a distinctive half-octagonal chimney feature on a limestone pedestal and console, gauged brick window voussoirs, granite sills and a round-headed door opening.
historical_significance: An unusual surviving mid-eighteenth-century townhouse whose distinctive chimney-like feature and doorway contribute to the historic character of Marlborough Street.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

name: 82 Marlborough Street
address: 82 Marlborough Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: End-of-terrace two-bay, three-storey house over a raised basement, built c.1810. NIAH records Flemish-bond red brickwork, granite ashlar basement, graduated window openings, a restrained doorcase with engaged pilasters and fanlight, granite entrance platform and wrought-iron railings on a granite plinth wall.
historical_significance: A Georgian townhouse retaining a strong combination of brick, granite, timber joinery and metal boundary details, all independently valuable for close-up field photography.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

name: Talbot House, 9 Talbot Street
address: 9 Talbot Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: Symmetrical eleven-bay, three-storey building over an exposed basement, built in 1842 with a central seven-bay breakfront and two-bay wings added in 1859. NIAH describes granite ashlar at ground level, ruled-and-lined rendered upper walls, rusticated quoins, decorative frieze with rosettes and dentils, granite modillions, and iron rainwater goods.
historical_significance: A substantial mid-nineteenth-century institutional building with unusually rich masonry and decorative details, documenting the architectural development of Talbot Street.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

name: National Model Schools, Marlborough Street — main school building
address: Marlborough Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: Detached seven-bay, three-storey former college building over an exposed basement, built c.1838, with a rectilinear entrance porch. NIAH describes an ashlar granite front elevation, dentillated granite cornice, moulded granite sill courses and detailed masonry articulation.
historical_significance: A significant nineteenth-century institutional building associated with the National Model Schools, retaining a carefully composed granite façade and substantial architectural detail.
access_status: Public-facing exterior or street object; respect private property, traffic, active transport infrastructure and any posted access restrictions.

name: Four Victorian cast-iron bollards, north end of O’Connell Street
address: Central mall at the north end of O’Connell Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: NIAH records a group of four cast-iron bollards on the central mall at the north end of O’Connell Street. The bollards are round in plan and approximately one metre high, with pinched cylindrical forms, decorative scrollwork, pierced openings and domed caps with foliate motifs. The inventory describes them as set in recent granite paving.
historical_significance: A surviving group of ornate Victorian street furniture contributing to the accumulated historic streetscape of O’Connell Street. NIAH suggests they may originally have functioned as air vents; this proposed function is not treated as certain.
access_status: Public central mall; photograph from pedestrian areas and remain clear of traffic, tram infrastructure and temporary restrictions.

name: Historic Custom House Docks boundary wall on Commons Street
address: Commons Street, beside Connolly Station, Dublin 1
historical_description: NIAH records a high limestone and granite boundary wall built circa 1830 along Commons Street at the rear of Connolly Station. Its fabric includes a rubble limestone lower section, a dressed granite string course, coursed dressed limestone blocks and granite coping. The record notes remains of former openings, later infill and a historic cobbled street surface with granite kerbs alongside the wall.
historical_significance: A surviving fragment of the former security boundary around the Custom House docks complex, documenting the industrial and commercial history of Dublin’s north quays. A local legend attributes the wall to French prisoners, but that story is not established by the inventory and is not presented as fact.
access_status: Photograph from lawful public viewpoints on Commons Street. Respect railway property, active transport operations and any barriers or access restrictions.
